newsitem.title: USA: U.S. fund managers upbeat on Hong Kong, China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. fund managers upbeat on Hong Kong, China.

text.p: Hong Kong and Chinese stocks carry tremendous potential for investors, with Britain's handover of the territory to China Monday, fund managers said.

However, they cautioned that the biggest question mark facing Hong Kong was whether communist China would keep intact the system of laws and free markets that has made Hong Kong one of the most attractive areas for investment in the world.
"In China, connections are still very important," said Mark Mobius, president of the Templeton Emerging Markets Fund.

"In my years in Hong Kong, (the authorities) fought for fairness and fair play. If that is not shown (under the Chinese), then the whole thing could unravel," said Mobius, who controls more than $10 billion in equity funds.

China took control of the booming territory at 1600 GMT Monday, ending 156 years of colonial rule. Hong Kong is now something of China's economic capital, attracting investors drawn by China's market of 1.2 billion people.
Some analysts have said that about 60 percent of direct foreign investment in China, or $100 billion, comes from Hong Kong.

Jan van Eck, executive vice president and emerging market strategist at Van Eck Global, an asset management firm in New York, said one of the attractive aspects about investing in Chinese and Hong Kong companies was China's strong economic growth.
China's economy has grown at eight or nine percent a year since 1978, and that rate should continue, van Eck said.
"The move to a market-based economy continues, if anything, at an accelerated pace," he said.

Noting the Hong Kong-based companies with Chinese financial backing, or so-called red chips, van Eck said they were "just another indication that the Chinese government is looking to market solutions for its growth goals.
"And I see no sign they will" reverse the trend, he added.

Thomas Tuttle, co-manager of the Colonial Newport Tiger Fund, which has 58 percent of its holdings in Hong Kong shares, said, "We think that the reversion to China will be the greatest stimulus to Hong Kong since the creation of the public markets." He added, "The opportunities now become almost unlimited. That's why there is so much excitement."
Tuttle recommended a blue-chip portfolio of banks and utilities, such as Hongkong Electric Holdings Ltd and Hang Seng Bank Ltd, as a solid long-term investement.
Power companies and banks are particularly attractive because of the long-term growth prospects in China, he said.
"This is a sure-fire way to make money. You don't have to get cute," he said.
